findings.question: When a large company reports earnings, do stocks with similar hidden exposures move with it?
findings.result: Yes, slightly: similar stocks moved the same way, beyond what sector explains, and shuffled scores do not reproduce it.
caveats: Calendar weeks are a coarse way to account for days that share market conditions.
The exposure scores are AI drafts that no person has reviewed.

findings.question: Do the hidden-exposure scores describe stocks better than sector labels?
findings.result: Exposure scores did a little better on average but not consistently.
caveats: Both are fitted on the same day they are measured on, so this is not a forecast.
Both figures are adjusted for how many columns each uses, and daily stock moves are mostly noise.
The exposure scores are AI drafts that no person has reviewed.

findings.question: Do earnings days move stocks by more than an ordinary day?
findings.result: Yes: far more earnings days than chance would give moved the stock by more than twice its normal noise.
caveats: The market is an equal-weighted average of other S&P 500 stocks, not an official index.
Prices come from an unofficial free source.
Direction is not tested here: the average abnormal return is close to zero because good and bad news cancel.

findings.question: Do the AI-drafted exposure scores agree with a person who scored the same companies blind?
findings.result: Only 0 of the 33 gold-set companies have been scored blind so far; at least 10 are needed.
caveats: The gold set is the most traded companies in each sector, which are likely the easiest for both the AI and a person.
A person's scores are judgements too, not measurements; agreement shows consistency, not truth.
Kappa counts every force for every company, including the many both leave at zero.
